title: DIB-KSI Consolidated Dataset
status: working draft, published for adversarial comment
generated_note: Generated from the source registries. Do not hand-edit; edit the sources and regenerate.

ontology.basis: NIST SP 800-171 r2/r3 + 800-171A, 800-172/172A, 32 CFR 170, DFARS 252.204-7012, FedRAMP CR26 assurance-class semantics
ontology.purpose: A deterministic system of record for defense-industrial-base CUI assurance. Entities and relations are the source; every deliverable (SDR/SSP, responsibility matrix, POA&M, affirmation package, dataflow diagram) is a projection over this graph. Nothing is authored twice, and no document can age into truth.
first_principles: Start with the data. What is it, why do you hold it, and can you hold less of it?
Then the people, processes, and technology that touch it — and only those.
Then who has access, on what basis, reviewed when.
Then the signal that proves the safeguard is running, not the narrative that says it was designed.
Then the claim, which is only ever as good as its newest supporting measurement.

layers.L0_obligation: What the law and the standard require. Stable across tenants; published, versioned, and identical for everyone.
layers.L1_data: What data exists, why it is held, where it lives, and how it moves. The scoping layer.
layers.L2_ppt: The people, processes, and technology that safeguard the data, and the access grants that connect people to it.
layers.L3_signal: The measured operational reality. Indicators, thresholds, measurements, collectors, findings.
layers.L4_assurance: The claims made from signals, who owns each one, what is inherited, and the human attestation on top.

Authority.definition: A statute, regulation, or contract clause that creates an obligation.

Requirement.definition: A single security requirement in the assessable baseline. The unit at which POA&M eligibility binds under 32 CFR 170.21.

fields.poam_eligible: boolean — per 170.21 and the DoD scoring methodology

AssessmentObjective.definition: A determination statement from 800-171A / 800-172A. THE GRADING UNIT. Every status the framework reports is ultimately per-AO.

fields.text_ref: pointer to the published objective; normative text is never reproduced here
fields.automatable: boolean — whether operational telemetry can demonstrate it

KSI.definition: Key Security Indicator. THE VALIDATION AND REPORTING UNIT. A capability that, when validated, demonstrates a set of AOs. A KSI is never the grading unit — it is MET only when every AO it maps is demonstrated.

fields.uplift: boolean — never required below Class D, never affects level compliance

KSIFamily.definition: Grouping of KSIs, e.g. IAM, MLA, SCB.

DataType.definition: A classification of data that drives obligation. The first question of the framework.

DataAsset.definition: A store or collection holding data of a given type. Carries the minimization record: why this data is held at all.

fields.necessity: object {basis, contract_ref, reviewed_on} — the answer to 'why do you have it'; absent necessity is a finding, not a footnote

DataFlow.definition: A declared movement of data between components, parties, or boundaries. Declared flows are claims; observed flows are signal. Disagreement is a finding.

Boundary.definition: An assessment boundary: the set of assets in scope for a given contract obligation.

fields.hosting: enum hosting_model — the enclave-hosted vs contractor-hosted distinction

Enclave.definition: A hardened multi-tenant environment operated by a provider, into which a tenant moves CUI and from which the tenant inherits controls and their proof. The defended-enclave deployment pattern for small and mid-size contractors.

fields.assurance_class: enum class — the class the enclave itself sustains
fields.crm_ref: pointer to the provider responsibility matrix
fields.validation_feed: object {endpoint, signing_key_id, cadence_days, last_received} — the machine-readable feed that makes inheritance real rather than asserted

Party.definition: An organization: the contractor (tenant), an external service provider, a cloud service provider, an enclave operator, an assessor, or the government.

Person.definition: A named human. Attestation, adjudication, and approval always resolve to a Person — never to a system or an agent.

Role.definition: A function a person holds, carrying privileges and obligations (e.g. Affirming Official, system administrator, CUI custodian).

Process.definition: An operational procedure people perform. Bound intent (E3) attaches here, never free-floating policy prose.

Component.definition: A technology asset in or adjacent to the boundary, categorized per 32 CFR 170.19.

fields.category_status: enum determination_status — categorization is a human determination

AccessGrant.definition: A person's access to a data asset, at a privilege level, on a stated basis, reviewed on a cadence. This entity is the 'who has access' first principle made queryable; it is not derived from a document.

fields.basis: string — the need that justifies it

Indicator.definition: A named, measurable property of the running environment — the unit of assurance. Defined once in the signal registry, with a unit, a subject population, a collection method, and per-class thresholds.

Measurement.definition: One timestamped observation of an Indicator, attributed to a Collector and an authoritative source. Measurements are facts; everything above them is inference.

fields.source: string — the authoritative API or system queried
fields.population: object {measured, total} — denominators are published, never implied

Collector.definition: The mechanism that produced a measurement: a platform-lane integration, a provider feed, or a human observation record.

fields.independence_group: string — two measurements from the same group are not independent methods

Threshold.definition: The bar an indicator must clear at a given assurance class. Thresholds are published policy, not per-tenant negotiation.

Finding.definition: A breach of a threshold, a stale claim, or a reconciliation disagreement. Findings are generated, never authored.

Claim.definition: An assertion that an assessment objective is satisfied, with its supporting measurements and evidence, its owner, and its freshness. A claim is a computed state, not a written statement.

fields.supported_by: array of ref Measurement or EvidenceRef
fields.last_supported_at: datetime — freshness is part of the claim, not metadata about it

EvidenceRef.definition: A pointer to an evidence object in the tenant's trust center, typed E1–E5. Evidence stays home; only the pointer and its hash travel.

fields.supports: array of ref KSI or ref Measurement — which claims this artifact underwrites
fields.measurement: optional ref Measurement — when the artifact backs a specific reading
fields.third_party: boolean — preferred for E2 at Class C and above
fields.adversarial: boolean — Class D adversarial demonstration marker for E5

ResponsibilityAssignment.definition: Who carries a given KSI or objective: the tenant, the enclave or provider, or both. This is the shared-responsibility split expressed as data rather than as a matrix document — the matrix is a projection of these records.

fields.provider: ref Party or ref Enclave, when mode is inherited or shared
fields.tenant_residual: string — what the tenant still owns when mode is shared
fields.basis: string — the CRM clause or authorization that supports the claim of inheritance

Exception.definition: A clocked, prioritized remediation record opened from a finding. Eligibility binds at the requirement level per 32 CFR 170.21; the engine, not a human narrative, decides eligibility.

Attestation.definition: A named human's signature on a stated posture at a stated time. The only entity in the ontology that cannot be computed.

fields.posture_hash: string — binds the signature to the exact computed state signed

invariants.statement: A KSI is MET only when every assessment objective it validates is demonstrated by the evidence types its assurance class requires. The objective is the grading unit; the KSI is the validation and reporting unit.
invariants.enforced_by: validator: ksi_status derived from claims, never asserted directly
invariants.plain: You do not get credit for a protection by saying you have it. The system works out whether you have met it from the evidence underneath, one assessment objective at a time.
invariants.without_it: Self-graded compliance. A summary page reads MET while nothing underneath actually supports it, which is the failure mode of every checklist ever filled in the night before an audit.
invariants.example: A shop marks access control as handled. The model does not accept the assertion. It checks each objective the indicator covers, finds one with no supporting evidence, and reports the indicator as not met — naming the objective that failed.
invariants.checked: Status is always computed from the evidence. There is no field anywhere in the model that lets a status be typed in directly.

invariants.statement: A coverage requirement applies to every in-scope subject. An uncovered subject is permitted only by a justified, dated exception that has not expired. No aggregate percentage is published, because no authority publishes one.
invariants.enforced_by: tools/lib.mjs — coverage evaluation; an unjustified or expired exception breaches the signal
invariants.plain: Every in-scope thing has to be covered. There is no passing score below all of them — but there is a documented exception with a name, a reason, and an expiry date.
invariants.without_it: Ninety-seven percent coverage forever, with the same three machines uncovered every quarter, because nobody can see which three they are.
invariants.example: A 12-person shop with one uncovered laptop and a 400-person firm with twelve are held to the same rule. Both must name the specific machines. The small shop fixes it that afternoon; the large one files dated exceptions for the four awaiting replacement and fixes the other eight.
invariants.checked: A reading that leaves a subject uncovered must carry an exception naming that subject, giving a reason, and carrying a future expiry date. An expired exception stops working on its expiry date without anyone intervening.

invariants.statement: Every deliverable is a projection over this graph. The Security Decision Record, the responsibility matrix, the POA&M, the dataflow diagram, and the affirmation package are views — none is a source, and none may contain a fact that is not derivable from entities and relations.
invariants.enforced_by: validator: no deliverable entity type exists; projections are computed by tools/project.mjs
invariants.plain: Every report is generated from the same underlying data. Nothing is typed by hand into a deliverable.
invariants.without_it: The security plan says one thing, the remediation tracker says another, and the responsibility matrix says a third — all describing the same environment, all edited at different times by different people.
invariants.example: Reclassify one folder as controlled information. The responsibility matrix, the remediation list, the dataflow diagram, and the decision record all change together, because each is computed from that same fact rather than transcribed from it.
invariants.checked: There is no deliverable stored anywhere in the model. Reports exist only as computations over the graph, so a report cannot contain a fact the graph does not hold.

invariants.statement: A claim on an automatable objective is met only while a supporting measurement exists inside the class cadence window. When the newest support ages past the window the claim becomes stale, not met. Documents cannot age into truth.
invariants.enforced_by: validator: freshness check against Indicator.cadence_days for the tenant class
invariants.plain: A claim is only good while the reading behind it is fresh. Past its shelf life it reports stale — not passing, not failing.
invariants.without_it: Documents that age into truth. A statement written in March still reads as current in December, and nothing in the process ever asks whether it still is.
invariants.example: Multi-factor enforcement is verified in March against a 30-day window. Through April the claim holds. In May, with no new reading, it goes stale on its own — nobody has to notice or decide to admit it.
invariants.checked: Each measurement declares how long a reading stays good, per assurance class. The claim is compared against the newest supporting reading every time anything is computed.

invariants.statement: A tenant may mark an objective inherited only when all three tests pass: the provider's authorization covers it, the provider emits a machine-readable validation for it on the tenant's class cadence, and no tenant-side configuration overrides it. A failed test degrades the assignment to shared or tenant; it never silently stands.
invariants.enforced_by: validator: three-test rule on every ResponsibilityAssignment with mode inherited
invariants.plain: You only get to say your provider handles something when three things are true at once, and the model re-checks all three every time rather than taking your word for it.
invariants.without_it: Inheritance by assumption, which is the most common way an enclave arrangement fails. A tenant believes the provider covers something; the provider believes it is the tenant’s; nobody is doing it.
invariants.example: A provider covers disk encryption for everything inside the enclave. But a tenant setting still permits download to local machines, so the third test fails and the assignment degrades from inherited to shared automatically. The tenant did not have to spot it.
invariants.checked: Three tests: the provider’s authorization actually covers it, the provider sends a machine-readable validation on your cadence, and no setting on your side overrides it. Failing any one degrades the claim rather than leaving it standing.

invariants.statement: Every data asset classified CUI carries at least one access grant, and every access grant carries a stated basis and a review date inside the review window. Access without a basis is a finding.
invariants.plain: Everyone who can reach controlled information has a stated reason for that access and a date when someone last confirmed the reason still holds.
invariants.without_it: Access that accumulates. People change roles, projects end, contractors leave, and the permissions stay — the single most common path into these environments.
invariants.example: An engineer moved off a program eight months ago. Their access record has no reviewed date inside the window, so it surfaces as a finding rather than waiting for an annual review to catch it.
invariants.checked: Every piece of controlled information must have at least one access grant, and every grant must carry a basis and a review date inside the review window.

invariants.statement: Every data asset classified CUI carries a necessity record naming why the data is held and when that was last reviewed. Data held without a stated need is a finding, because the cheapest control is not holding the data.
invariants.plain: Every piece of controlled information you hold has to have a reason to be here, and a date when that reason was last checked.
invariants.without_it: Scope that only grows. Old programs, superseded drawing revisions, an attachment from 2021 — each one adding cost and risk while protecting nothing.
invariants.example: A closed contract’s drawing package has no current necessity record, so it is flagged. Deleting it removes the folder from scope altogether — there is then nothing to encrypt, nobody whose access needs reviewing, and no monitoring to keep running.
invariants.checked: Controlled information without a stated need is reported as a finding. This is the only rule here that removes risk rather than managing it.

invariants.statement: Two measurements read from the same control plane do not count as two independent methods for Class C and above.
invariants.plain: Two readings from the same place are one reading. Buying a second tool that asks the same system the same question does not give you a second opinion.
invariants.without_it: The appearance of corroboration without any. Two products, one blind spot, and a shared failure nobody can see from inside either of them.
invariants.example: Querying an identity system directly and running a second tool that queries the same identity system is one reading, twice. Pairing that identity query with a log platform holding authentication records is genuinely two, because the log platform would have to be independently wrong to agree.
invariants.checked: Each collector declares which control plane it reads from. Readings only count separately when those differ. Required from assurance Class C upward.

invariants.statement: Attestation, adjudication, categorization confirmation, and risk acceptance resolve to a named Person. No computed state substitutes for a signature, and every signature binds by hash to the exact posture signed.
invariants.plain: A person signs. Nothing computed ever substitutes for that signature, and the signature is bound to the exact state that was signed.
invariants.without_it: Accountability that dissolves into the system. Everyone points at the dashboard and nobody has actually accepted the risk.
invariants.example: The environment changes after an attestation is signed. The signature no longer matches the current state, so it does not carry forward. Someone has to look at what changed and sign again.
invariants.checked: Attestation, adjudicating a finding, confirming what counts as controlled information, and accepting risk each resolve to a named person, and each signature is bound by hash to the posture it covers.

invariants.statement: Every measurement either cites an external authority for its requirement, or is explicitly marked as this project’s own policy choice with a stated rationale. A number with no stated origin is not allowed.
invariants.enforced_by: tools/test.mjs — INV-AUTHORITY block; the suite fails if any signal has neither an authority nor a local-policy rationale
invariants.plain: Every number either cites where it came from, or openly admits it is this project’s own judgment. There is no third option.
invariants.without_it: Invented precision. A threshold that looks authoritative, gets quoted, gets built into somebody’s contract, and traces back to nothing at all.
invariants.example: The standing administrator count cites a published baseline that sets a floor of two and a ceiling of eight. The detection-time target cites nothing, because no authority publishes one, so it is labelled as our judgment with the reasoning attached. Eleven of the twenty-two measurements fall on each side.
invariants.checked: A measurement must carry either a citation to an external source or a written rationale for the choice. One with neither stops the build.

invariants.statement: A KSI’s evidence_depth is met only when persistent measurements and EvidenceRefs satisfy the machine-checkable evidence_floors for the tenant’s assurance class. Signal status and evidence depth are separate; a passing bar with thin evidence reports depth short, never depth met.
invariants.enforced_by: tools/lib.mjs — evaluateEvidenceFloor; validator INV-EVIDENCE-FLOOR; tools/test.mjs negative cases
invariants.plain: Clearing a numeric bar is not the same as bringing the proof your class demands. The floor says which evidence types and how many independent methods you need; depth reports whether you have them.
invariants.without_it: A green MFA reading from one API, treated as Class C complete, while the second independent method and the bound-intent artifact were never collected.
invariants.example: At Class C an identity KSI needs two independent E1 readings plus an E3 bound-intent record. Dual MFA telemetry without the E3 artifact keeps claim status met if the bar clears, but evidence_depth stays short until the bound policy is hashed in.
invariants.checked: evidence_depth met requires floor_met with no missing_types. Reporting met depth without the floor is a validation error.

scenarios.statement: The same rules land very differently depending on what you have and how you have arranged it. These three are computed from the registries, not estimated — change an assignment and these numbers move.
scenarios.caveat: Illustrative shapes, not advice about your situation. Your class is set by your contract, and your scope is set by where your controlled information actually lives, which is often not where people think it lives.

cases.name: 12-person machine shop, everything inside a rented enclave
cases.situation: One prime, one program. Drawings arrive by secure transfer and are opened only inside a rented environment through a thin client. Nothing lands on the shop floor machines. Two people have admin rights, one of them the owner.
cases.what_you_run: Effectively nothing of your own. The provider supplies the readings for what it operates. You need a way to record training completions, a way to show you exercised the incident reporting path, and someone to sign.
cases.first_finding: Almost always the same one: a former employee or an outside accountant still has an account nobody disabled. It is the cheapest finding to fix and the most common way these environments are actually breached.
cases.hardest_part: Believing the enclave is enough and resisting the urge to "just email that one file" to somebody. One download reverses the entire scope reduction.

cases.name: 200-person manufacturer, enclave plus managed laptops
cases.situation: Multiple programs, an engineering team that needs controlled files locally for CAD work, and a corporate network alongside the enclave. Laptops are managed but they do process controlled data.
cases.what_you_run: Real infrastructure. Identity, endpoint protection, vulnerability management, log retention, and a way to prove two of those read from genuinely different places, because Class C requires a second independent reading.
cases.first_finding: Endpoint coverage measured against the wrong denominator. The endpoint console reports every machine healthy, and it is right — about the machines it knows about. The four that never got enrolled are invisible to it by construction.
cases.hardest_part: The jump from one reading to two independent ones. Buying a second tool that queries the same system does not satisfy it, and that surprises people who have already spent the money.

cases.name: Subcontractor with controlled data spread across three clouds
cases.situation: Grew by acquisition. Controlled information lives in a general-purpose cloud file share, an object storage bucket, and an engineering SaaS tool nobody put through review. No enclave, and no arrangement anywhere that is scoped to controlled defense information specifically.
cases.what_you_run: More than the other two, but the surprise is what the providers already do for you and why you still cannot claim it. Roughly half the catalogue lands as shared: the provider supplies the capability and you configure it. Identity, encryption at rest, audit logging, and durability all work this way. You run the configuration and the reading; they run the machinery underneath.
cases.first_finding: The framework refuses to model the environment cleanly, and that refusal is the finding. Controlled information sitting in a third location with no stated reason fails the minimisation rule before a single security control is assessed.
cases.hardest_part: Understanding why so little is inherited when the provider does so much. It is not that they are doing nothing — they run the datacenter, the hypervisor, and the physical destruction of failed drives, and no customer can re-perform any of that. It is that a commercial arrangement does not emit a machine-readable validation about your data on your cadence. An annual audit report is a point-in-time artifact about the provider, not a continuous reading about you, so the three-test rule lands it as shared rather than inherited.
cases.inheritance_note: Four indicators are genuinely inherited: datacenter physical access, environmental protection, and the physical media lifecycle inside the provider estate. Thirty-three are shared. That shared column is the honest picture of commercial cloud — the provider is doing real work, and you still own the configuration, the evidence, and the answer.

scenarios.reading_the_numbers: The second and third shapes are both Class C; they differ in whether an arrangement scoped to controlled information emits evidence on a cadence. That difference moves work between columns without changing what any provider physically does.

evidence_types.statement: Five kinds of evidence, ordered by how hard they are to fake and how much work they are to produce. Assurance classes differ mainly in which of these they will accept: lower classes take an assertion backed by configuration, higher classes want telemetry and a demonstration.

types.name: Machine telemetry
types.what: A reading taken directly from the running system, by querying its live state rather than describing it.
types.strong: It reflects what is true at the moment of the query, cannot be backdated, and can be re-taken by somebody else who will get the same answer.
types.weak: It says nothing about what was true yesterday, and it inherits the blind spots of whatever produced it. A reading that covers only the assets the tool already knows about is measuring the tool.

examples.example: The provider’s feed reports that multi-factor authentication is enforced for all six accounts that can reach the enclave, listing the six.
A query against the endpoint platform returns agent status for 214 machines, checked against an asset inventory of 218 — and names the four that are missing.
Three separate queries, one per provider, returning encryption state per storage location. The reading is only as good as the list of locations, which is the part that is actually wrong here.

types.mistake: Presenting a dashboard screenshot as telemetry. A screenshot is a picture of a reading, not the reading, and nobody can re-derive it.

types.name: Provenanced artifact
types.what: A document or export that carries proof of where it came from and that it has not been altered since — a signature, a hash chain, a trusted timestamp. Best when it originates from somebody other than the party being assessed.
types.strong: It survives the passage of time and the departure of the person who produced it. A third-party-originated artifact is the hardest kind of evidence to quietly improve.
types.weak: It is true as of its date and silent afterward. It also proves the artifact is intact, not that its contents were correct when written.

examples.example: The provider’s signed attestation of the environment, with a certificate covering the specific offering the shop is using rather than the provider’s brand generally.
A signed export of the quarterly access review, hashed and timestamped when the reviewer approved it, so a later edit is detectable.

Three annual audit reports from three providers. Each is a legitimate provenanced artifact and none of them says anything about this tenant’s data specifically — which is exactly why they support shared responsibility rather than inheritance.

types.mistake: Treating a vendor’s compliance certificate as covering your usage. Certificates cover a defined service in a defined configuration, and the thing you bought may sit outside it.

types.name: Bound intent
types.what: A short policy statement wired to the configuration that enforces it, so the rule and its enforcement point at each other.
types.strong: It closes the oldest gap in compliance, where the written policy and the running system drift apart for years without anyone noticing.
types.weak: It proves the rule is wired up, not that the wiring covers everything. A policy bound to one system and silent about three others looks identical from the policy side.

examples.example: A one-paragraph rule stating controlled drawings never leave the enclave, bound to the platform setting that blocks download, print, and removable media — so turning the setting off breaks the stated policy visibly.
A change-control rule bound to the branch protection and required-review settings that enforce it, rather than a procedure document describing what reviewers are supposed to do.
The failure case. A data-handling policy exists and binds to nothing, because there is no single enforcement point that covers all three locations. The absence of a binding is the finding.

types.mistake: Writing the policy and the configuration separately and asserting they agree. If nothing breaks when they diverge, they will diverge.

types.name: Human observation
types.what: Somebody looked, asked, or walked the floor, and wrote down what they found — interviews, walkthroughs, physical inspections.
types.strong: It reaches everything no query can see: whether people understand the rule, whether the shortcut everyone takes matches the documented process, whether the locked room is actually locked.
types.weak: It does not scale, it is a snapshot, and its quality depends entirely on who did the looking and what they wrote down.

examples.example: A walkthrough confirming the two machines with enclave access sit in the locked office rather than on the shop floor, with the date, the observer, and what was seen.

Interviews with four engineers about how they actually move CAD files between the enclave and their laptops. This surfaces the workaround that telemetry cannot see because the workaround is compliant-looking.
Asking the engineering team which systems hold controlled information. This is how the third cloud gets discovered, because nobody put it through review and so it appears in no inventory.

types.mistake: Recording the conclusion without the observation. "Confirmed compliant" is not evidence; what the observer saw, on what date, is.

types.name: Demonstration
types.what: The capability is exercised under realistic conditions and the results are measured. Not a description of what would happen — a record of what did.
types.strong: It is the only evidence that distinguishes a capability that exists from one that works. Restore procedures and incident reporting paths fail here constantly, and it is far better to find that out on a Tuesday.
types.weak: Expensive, and easy to stage into meaninglessness. A restore test against a small file on a good day proves less than the effort suggests.

examples.example: Walking the incident reporting path end to end without filing a real report: who is called, what the reporting portal needs, and whether anybody has the credentials to submit within the required window.

A restore of a controlled-data volume to a stated recovery objective, timed, with the actual duration recorded — including the part where the restore succeeded but took eleven hours against a four-hour objective.

A tabletop asking a simple question: controlled data is exposed in one of the three locations, who is called and within what deadline. The exercise usually establishes that nobody is sure which contract clause applies.

types.mistake: Running the demonstration and recording only that it passed. The measured result is the evidence, and a failed demonstration honestly recorded is worth more than a staged success.

evidence_types.how_classes_differ: Higher assurance classes do not ask for more paperwork, they ask for evidence further down this list. A class that accepts bound intent alone is asking whether you set it up. A class that wants telemetry plus a demonstration is asking whether it still works and whether you have proved it recently.

working_sets.statement: The catalogue is exhaustive so the model can be correct about any arrangement. No single organisation is expected to hold it in its head. This is what each of the three shapes actually touches.
working_sets.point: The reference is large. The work is not.

signals.premise: The unit of assurance is the signal, not the document. Each indicator names a measurable property of the running environment, the population it is measured over, the method that produces it, how fresh it must be at each assurance class, and the bar it must clear. A claim supported only by prose is not a claim this framework can grade.

conventions.population: Every percentage publishes its denominator. A measurement without {measured, total} is rejected by the validator, because a coverage number over an undefined population is not a measurement.
conventions.thresholds: Coverage requirements are universal: the requirement applies to every in-scope subject, and any uncovered subject must carry a justified, dated exception. No aggregate percentage is published, because no authority publishes one — CISA, CIS, DISA and Microsoft all use per-item pass/fail plus documented exceptions.
conventions.cadence: cadence_days is the maximum age of the newest supporting measurement before the claim it supports goes stale (INV-SIGNAL). It tightens by class: A at affirmation, B monthly, C every three days, D daily.
conventions.independence: At Class C and above two automated methods must come from collectors in different independence groups. Two queries against the same control plane are one method.
conventions.authority: Every signal either cites an external authority or is explicitly flagged derived: local-policy with a rationale. The CI suite fails if a signal has neither (INV-AUTHORITY).

signals.subject: All identities with access to CUI assets, measured against the total identity population in scope

responsibility_patterns.premise: A defended enclave is a deployment pattern, not a product. This file expresses the shared-responsibility split as data so a tenant's responsibility matrix is generated from its architecture rather than transcribed from a provider's PDF. Modes are defaults for a tenant that has actually moved its CUI into the enclave; the validator re-tests every inherited assignment against the three-test rule before it will grade one.

three_test_rule.statement: An objective may be marked inherited only when all three tests pass. A failed test degrades the assignment to shared or tenant. Inheritance is never a status a tenant simply declares.

tests.test: The provider's authorization and responsibility matrix cover the objective at or above the tenant's assurance class.
The provider emits a machine-readable, signed validation for the objective within the tenant's class cadence (SIG-INHERIT-FRESH).
No tenant-side configuration, export, or endpoint re-scopes the objective back to the tenant — a tenant that pulls CUI out of the enclave has re-scoped the destination back in.

three_test_rule.note: T3 is the test tenants fail most. The enclave carries the control only for the CUI actually inside it.

enclave-only.name: Enclave-only (thin client, no local CUI landing)
enclave-only.description: All CUI processing occurs inside the enclave. Endpoints render but never store CUI; download, print, and removable media are blocked at the platform. This is the pattern with the largest scope reduction and the one most small contractors should target.

enclave-plus-endpoints.name: Enclave plus managed endpoints
enclave-plus-endpoints.description: CUI is centered in the enclave, but managed tenant endpoints process some CUI locally. Every objective that touches the endpoint returns to the tenant or becomes shared.

commercial-cloud.name: Commercial cloud and SaaS, no dedicated enclave
commercial-cloud.description: Controlled information sits in general-purpose cloud storage, SaaS applications, and tenant-managed infrastructure. The provider genuinely operates a large part of the stack, but nothing in the arrangement is scoped to controlled defense information specifically, and the provider does not emit per-tenant validation on a cadence.
commercial-cloud.inheritance_reality: A great deal is inheritable in principle and fails on evidence. A major provider really does run the datacenter, the hypervisor, and the physical media lifecycle, and no customer can or should re-perform those. What a commercial arrangement generally does not do is emit a machine-readable validation per tenant on your cadence. An annual audit report is a point-in-time artifact about the provider, not a continuous reading about your data, so most of what the provider genuinely does lands as shared rather than inherited under the three-test rule. That is a statement about evidence flow, not about whether the provider is competent.

evidence_flow.statement: Inheritance is only real when the proof travels with the control. The provider validation feed is the mechanism.
steps: The provider runs collectors for the controls it operates and computes its own per-objective claim states, exactly as a tenant does.
It publishes a signed, machine-readable validation feed keyed by objective, carrying status, the class it sustains, the measurement timestamp, and a hash — never the underlying evidence.
The tenant ingests the feed, verifies the signature, and records provenance in its own manifest. Raw provider evidence stays with the provider; the tenant holds the attested claim and its pointer.
The tenant's validator re-runs the three-test rule on every inherited objective at ingest, and SIG-INHERIT-FRESH ages the whole inherited set together when the feed stops arriving.

The tenant's responsibility matrix, Security Decision Record, and posture rollup are then projections that already contain the inherited layer — nothing is transcribed, and a stale feed is visible as staleness rather than as silence.
evidence_flow.assessor_consequence: The assessor validates the provider's pipeline once and samples it, rather than re-walking the same inherited stack in every tenant. That single change is where population-scale assessment cost actually falls.

honest_boundary.statement: Inheritance shrinks the tenant's obligation; it never zeroes it, and this file is written so the residual is impossible to lose.
points: An unvalidated enclave inherits nothing. The provider must itself be assessed at or above the tenant's class.
The grading invariant does not relax for inherited controls: every mapped objective must still be demonstrated, by the provider rather than by nobody.
A tenant that exports CUI to an endpoint outside the enclave has re-scoped that endpoint back in, and the three-test rule will fail T3 rather than let the claim stand.
Personnel, training, marking judgment, incident reporting, governance, log review, scope declaration, and the affirmation itself never inherit.

Concentration is a real trade: enclaves reduce sprawl across thousands of under-resourced environments while increasing the consequence of one provider's failure. The framework's answer is that provider validation is continuous, machine-checked, and visible to every tenant at once — not that the trade does not exist.

collection.supersedes: ontology/collectors.json (0.3.0), which conflated three separate things: the baseline that defines a requirement, the method used to read state, and the product that happens to implement that method.
collection.premise: This framework does not maintain a list of approved products, and it should not be read as endorsing any tool named here. A measurement is fed by whatever can retrieve the state and emit a conforming reading — a vendor API, a webhook, an agent, a SIEM query, a CI job, a spreadsheet export, a script you wrote yourself. What the framework is definitive about is the shape of the reading and the assurance properties of the method that produced it. Anything meeting the interface below is a valid collector.

separation_of_concerns.statement: Three things get confused constantly, including by earlier versions of this file. They are separate and belong in separate fields.

concerns.answers: What does good look like, and who says so?
concerns.examples: CISA SCuBA secure configuration baselines, CIS Benchmarks, DISA STIGs, vendor security baselines, the CISA KEV catalogue, NIST CMVP, or your own documented policy.
concerns.note: SCuBA and CIS are baselines. They define the bar. They are not collectors, and a tool that ships a baseline is not the same thing as the baseline it ships.

concerns.answers: How is the state actually retrieved?
concerns.examples: Authenticated API pull, pushed webhook, agent self-report, log query, config scan, admission-control decision, pipeline gate, outside-in probe, system-of-record query, attested human record.
concerns.note: This is the part that determines assurance properties — provenance, independence, freshness — so this is the part the framework constrains.

concerns.examples: Anything. The list in this file is illustrative and deliberately incomplete.
concerns.note: Naming products per signal would date the framework within a release cycle and would quietly exclude every environment that made a different choice.

interface.statement: A collector is anything that emits this shape; nothing has to be registered, approved, or vendor-listed. If a reading carries these fields and can be re-derived from the source named in it, the framework will grade it.

required.description: When the state was read, not when the record was written.
One of the method ids below. Determines how independence and freshness are judged.
The system that produced it, specifically enough that somebody else could go re-read the same thing.
The denominator, and where it came from. For coverage measurements this must be the authoritative inventory, never the reporting tool's own list of things it already knows about.

conditional.description: Named subjects not covered. Named, because a percentage cannot be remediated.
Each carrying a justification and an expiry date.

optional.description: Signature, hash, transcript, or query text — whatever lets a reviewer reproduce the reading rather than trust it.
Pointer to the raw artifact in evidence storage.

interface.denominator_warning: The most common way an honest pipeline reports a false number: coverage computed against the tool's own inventory rather than the organisation's. An endpoint platform that reports 100% agent health across the endpoints it can see says nothing about the laptop that has never had the agent installed. Every coverage reading names where its denominator came from for exactly this reason.

methods.name: Authenticated API query against a control plane
methods.description: REST, GraphQL, SDK, or CLI query against the management plane that holds the state — an identity provider, cloud provider, SaaS admin API, MDM, EDR console, vulnerability platform, ticketing system, or anything else with an interface.
methods.freshness: on-demand, so cadence is whatever you schedule
methods.provenance: Strong when the query text and the response are both retained. Weak when only a summary is kept.
methods.control_plane: The queried platform. Two queries against the same platform are one reading for independence purposes, however different the tools issuing them.
methods.denominator_risk: high — the platform reports what it manages, which is rarely the whole estate

methods.name: Pushed event or webhook
methods.description: The source pushes state changes as they happen — webhooks, event buses, message queues, streaming telemetry, cloud audit event feeds.
methods.freshness: continuous, which makes drift visible between scheduled reads
methods.provenance: Strong for change detection, weak for current state. An event stream tells you what moved, not what is true now; pair it with a periodic pull.
methods.denominator_risk: very high — an absence of events is not evidence of compliance, it is equally consistent with a broken feed

methods.name: Agent on the asset reports its own state
methods.description: Endpoint agent, configuration management client, or host daemon reporting from the asset itself.
methods.provenance: Good for host-local facts no control plane can see. Circular for the question of whether the agent is installed, which is why agent coverage is measured against the inventory rather than against the agent fleet.
methods.control_plane: The asset, aggregated by its management console.
methods.denominator_risk: very high — an agent cannot report about a host it is not on

methods.name: Query over retained logs
methods.description: Search across a SIEM, log platform, data lake, or warehouse holding retained telemetry.
methods.freshness: bounded by ingestion lag and retention window
methods.provenance: Strong when the query is retained with the result. This is usually the only method that can answer historical questions, which is what the higher assurance classes ask for.
methods.control_plane: The log platform, which is often independent of the system that generated the events — one of the few genuinely independent second reads available.
methods.denominator_risk: high — you can only query what was onboarded, and log source coverage is itself a measurement

methods.name: Assessment against structured content
methods.description: A host, image, container, or configuration evaluated against machine-readable criteria content — SCAP, benchmark profiles, compliance-as-code profiles, image scanners.
methods.provenance: Strong. The content, the target, and the result together are reproducible.
methods.denominator_risk: moderate — scan scope is explicit, but unscanned assets are invisible

methods.name: Policy decision at admission time
methods.description: A policy engine evaluating a change as it is requested — Kubernetes admission, cloud policy engines, resource-level guardrails.
methods.freshness: continuous, at the moment of change
methods.provenance: Strong, and preventive rather than detective: it records what was refused, not just what exists.
methods.control_plane: The orchestrator or cloud control plane.
methods.denominator_risk: low for what it governs, total for what routes around it

methods.name: Gate in the build or deployment pipeline
methods.description: Evaluation of code, infrastructure-as-code, dependencies, or images before merge or release.
methods.provenance: Strong. The run is logged, attributable to a commit, and re-runnable.
methods.denominator_risk: moderate — governs what ships through the pipeline, not what was changed by hand

methods.name: Outside-in observation
methods.description: Observation requiring no privileged access — public DNS records, TLS configuration, certificate transparency, exposed service enumeration, breach and credential exposure feeds.
methods.provenance: Strong and adversary-equivalent: it sees what an attacker sees, and does not depend on the organisation's own instrumentation being honest or working.
methods.control_plane: None. Independent of every internal system, which makes it valuable as a second read.
methods.denominator_risk: low for what is externally visible, total for anything that is not

methods.name: Query against a system of record
methods.description: Process facts held in business systems — ticketing and change management, HR and directory records, learning management, asset and contract systems, procurement.
methods.freshness: as current as the business process feeding it
methods.provenance: Good for process facts, and the only practical source for several human-centred requirements. It measures the record, not the reality behind it.
methods.denominator_risk: high — an incomplete roster produces a flattering training-coverage number

methods.name: Human-produced record with provenance
methods.description: Demonstrations, exercises, restore tests, walkthroughs, interviews, physical inspections, and reporting-path drills. Any requirement no query can answer.
methods.provenance: Depends entirely on what is retained. A dated record naming who did what, with the artifacts produced, is evidence. An assertion that it happened is not.
methods.note: Roughly a third of the catalogue is judgment, physical, or human. Naming this as a method keeps that honest instead of implying the whole framework is automated.

methods.name: Reading relayed from a provider
methods.description: A validated reading the tenant did not collect, delivered by a service provider for a control the provider operates. The collection happened on the provider side by some other method; this is the transport and the attestation around it.
methods.freshness: as fresh as the feed, which is itself a measurement — see SIG-INHERIT-FRESH
methods.provenance: Only as strong as what the feed carries. A signed reading naming the provider-side method and population is evidence; a green tile on a portal is not.
methods.control_plane: The provider. Independent of the tenant, and shared with every other tenant of that provider — which is why a provider-side failure is correlated across its customers rather than isolated.
methods.denominator_risk: high — the provider measures its own estate, and the tenant must confirm the reading covers the tenant’s controlled data specifically
methods.note: This is the method behind every inherited control. When the feed goes quiet everything inherited through it ages out together and reports stale, because the tenant has stopped receiving evidence the protection is running.

methods.name: Computed from other readings
methods.description: No independent collection. The value is a function of other measurements already in the graph.
methods.freshness: inherits the oldest input, and goes stale when any input does
methods.provenance: Only as good as its inputs, and it must name them.
methods.control_plane: Inherits from inputs, and therefore never counts as an independent second read.

independence.statement: Class C and above require two independent methods per automatable indicator. Independence is structural, not a matter of running two products.
independence.rule: Two readings are independent when they originate from different control planes. Different methods against the same control plane are a weaker form and count only where noted; the same method against the same control plane never counts twice.

worked_examples.pair: Identity provider API + a tool that queries the same identity provider
worked_examples.why: One control plane. Two vendors reading the same tenant configuration produce one fact, twice.

worked_examples.pair: Identity provider API + SIEM query over authentication logs
worked_examples.why: Different control planes, and the log platform would have to be independently wrong to agree.

worked_examples.pair: Endpoint agent self-report + asset inventory from the network or procurement side
worked_examples.why: This is the pairing that catches the machine with no agent, which is the only interesting case.

worked_examples.pair: Internal TLS configuration scan + external probe of the same endpoint
worked_examples.why: The external view does not depend on internal instrumentation working or being truthful.

worked_examples.pair: Two cloud security tools reading the same account
worked_examples.why: Same control plane. Broad coverage is not the same property as independence.

criteria_sources.statement: What a reading is evaluated against. These define the bar; they do not collect anything. A signal cites one of these in its authority field, or declares itself a local policy choice.

sources.name: CISA SCuBA Secure Configuration Baselines
sources.form: policy statements with SHALL / SHOULD criticality
sources.note: Binding on federal civilian agencies under BOD 25-01; recommended by CISA for all stakeholders.

sources.name: CIS Benchmarks
sources.covers: operating systems, cloud providers, platforms, containers
sources.form: consensus configuration benchmarks with profile levels
sources.note: Widely adopted and broad, but licensed content — check terms before redistributing.

sources.name: DISA STIGs and SRGs
sources.note: Not required by CMMC or 800-171. Frequently assumed to be; it is worth checking your contract rather than your instincts.

sources.name: Vendor security baselines
sources.form: recommended configuration published by the platform owner
sources.note: Authoritative about intent, and sometimes weaker than an independent baseline about risk.

sources.name: CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalogue
sources.form: an enumerated list with remediation due dates

sources.name: NIST Cryptographic Module Validation Program
sources.form: certificate records with operational environment bounds and status
sources.note: Status matters as much as the certificate: sunset, historical, and revoked modules still appear in search results.

sources.name: Contract clauses
sources.note: The only category here that is legally binding on its own.

sources.name: Local policy
sources.covers: anything no external authority sets a bar for
sources.form: documented internal decision with a rationale
sources.note: Half the measurements in this framework fall here, and each says so rather than implying an authority it does not have.

example_implementations.statement: ILLUSTRATIVE AND DELIBERATELY INCOMPLETE. Not endorsements, not requirements, not a shortlist. They exist to answer 'what would this look like in practice' for someone who has not built a pipeline before, and they will date faster than anything else in this repository. Any product, script, or platform meeting the interface above is equally valid, including one you write yourself.

by_method.platform-api: Identity providers, cloud provider APIs, MDM and UEM consoles, EDR platforms, vulnerability management platforms, SaaS admin APIs, CSPM and CNAPP tools, backup platforms, or a script hitting any of the same endpoints. Baseline-evaluating tools such as ScubaGear, ScubaGoggles, CIS-CAT, and open-source cloud scanners also sit here — each is one implementation that bundles a criteria source with an API pull.
by_method.event-stream: Cloud audit event feeds, SaaS webhooks, message queues, streaming telemetry pipelines, alerting integrations.
by_method.agent-report: Endpoint detection agents, configuration management clients, host compliance daemons, patch management clients.
by_method.log-query: SIEM platforms, log analytics services, data warehouses and lakehouses holding retained telemetry.
by_method.config-scan: SCAP-based scanners, benchmark assessment tools, compliance-as-code profile runners, container and image scanners.
by_method.admission-control: Kubernetes admission controllers, cloud-native policy engines, resource guardrail services.
by_method.pipeline-check: Policy-as-code evaluators in CI, IaC scanners, dependency and secret scanners, signed-build attestation.
by_method.external-probe: DNS and TLS inspection, certificate transparency monitoring, attack-surface management services, credential exposure feeds.
by_method.record-system: Ticketing and change management, HR and directory systems, learning management platforms, asset and contract registers.
by_method.attested-record: Exercise reports, restore-test records, walkthrough notes, signed inspection records — structured into the reading shape rather than filed as prose.
by_method.derived: Your own computation over readings already in the graph.

known_traps.detail: Tools that were freely available can move behind a licence. Check the current terms rather than the blog post that recommended it.
Several widely cited scanners are archived, folded into other products, or closed to new customers. A GitHub star count is not a maintenance signal.
Some publishers label their own tools alpha. Treat results as indicative until they say otherwise.

known_traps.trap: Exit codes that mean scan health
known_traps.detail: Some tools return success when the scan completed, regardless of what it found. Wiring that into a gate produces a permanently green pipeline.
Only a minority of published hardening guides ship machine-readable content, so automated coverage of a benchmark is usually narrower than the benchmark itself.

guidance.premise: An indicator statement says what must be true. It does not tell a reader what doing it looks like, what they would hand over, or how anyone would check it without a person in the loop. This file answers those four questions in plain language for the indicators a tenant owns alone, because those are the ones where the reader personally has to act.
guidance.coverage_note: Deliberately incomplete. Written first for the fifteen indicators a small contractor owns alone under the enclave-only profile, which is the most common shape in this sector and the one the enclave argument points at. Indicators that are shared or inherited are driven by a provider, and guidance for them is worth writing only after this set has survived contact with real practitioners. The test suite reports coverage rather than letting the gap go unnoticed.

fields.question: What is actually being asked, phrased so somebody who does not work in compliance can answer yes, partly, or no.
fields.in_place: What the implemented state looks like concretely. Not the goal — the arrangement.
fields.evidence: What you would put in front of an assessor. Artifacts, not assertions.
fields.check: How the reading is taken without a person, and what makes it fail. Where a control genuinely cannot be automated, this says so instead of pretending.

KSI-CED-CUI.question: Does everyone who touches controlled information know what it is, how to handle it, and what to do if a colleague starts behaving strangely around it?
KSI-CED-CUI.in_place: One short course covering what controlled information is, how it is marked, what handling rules apply, and how to raise a concern about someone's behaviour. Delivered on hire and repeated annually. The roster it is measured against comes from HR, not from the training platform's own user list.
KSI-CED-CUI.evidence: The course content, showing it covers both handling and insider-threat awareness. A completion record per person with dates. The roster the completion was measured against, and where that roster came from.
KSI-CED-CUI.check: Query the training platform for completions per person, then join to the HR roster. Anyone on the roster without a completion inside the window is named. Measuring against the platform's own user list instead of the roster is the classic way this reports a flattering number. The query proves attendance and nothing else — whether the training taught the right things stays human judgment.

KSI-CED-RAT.question: Do you check whether the training worked, or only that people clicked through it?
KSI-CED-RAT.in_place: Somebody reviews both completion and effect — phishing simulation results, whether incidents keep tracing to the same misunderstanding — and changes the training when it is not landing. A completion rate on its own measures attendance.
KSI-CED-RAT.evidence: A dated review naming who did it, what they looked at, and what changed as a result. A review that changed nothing, with a stated reason, is still evidence; a review with no record is not.
KSI-CED-RAT.check: Partly automatable. Completion and phishing click-rate trends are queryable; the judgment about whether the training is working is not. Record the review as a dated artifact and let the metrics feed it.

KSI-CMT-RVP.question: Does anyone check that the way changes actually get made matches the way you say they get made?
KSI-CMT-RVP.in_place: On a stated cadence, somebody takes a sample of changes that really happened and compares them against the documented process. The interesting output is the gap: emergency changes that skipped review, or a documented step nobody has performed in a year.
KSI-CMT-RVP.evidence: The dated review, the sample examined, and any discrepancies found with what was done about them.
KSI-CMT-RVP.check: Sample changes from the change or ticket system and compare each against the approvals the process requires. Changes with no approval record are named. That part is mechanical. The judgment the machine cannot make is whether a documented step is still worth having, or whether the process everyone actually follows is the better one.

KSI-CUI-MRK.question: When controlled information arrives, does a named person decide it is controlled, mark it, and does everyone know what that marking obliges them to do?
KSI-CUI-MRK.in_place: A named person confirms the designation rather than it being assumed. Marking follows a written standard. The handling rules attached to a marking are published somewhere the people who see the marking can find them.
KSI-CUI-MRK.evidence: Designation decisions with who made them and when. A sample of marked artifacts. The handling rule the marking points to.
KSI-CUI-MRK.check: Largely human, and honestly so — deciding what counts as controlled is judgment. What is queryable: whether every registered controlled asset carries a designation record with a named confirmer and a date. Assets holding controlled information with no confirmer are named.

KSI-IAM-SUS.question: If an account starts behaving as though it has been stolen, does something actually happen — and how quickly?
KSI-IAM-SUS.in_place: Risk signals from the identity platform trigger a real consequence: blocked sign-in, forced re-authentication, or a disabled account. Either automatic, or a queue somebody genuinely watches. A risk score nobody acts on is telemetry, not a control.
KSI-IAM-SUS.evidence: The policy configuration showing what triggers what. A log of triggered events with what happened and how long it took.
KSI-IAM-SUS.check: Query the identity platform for risk-based policy state and for high-risk sign-ins that completed without a challenge. Any high-risk session that simply proceeded is the finding.

KSI-INR-AAR.question: After something goes wrong, does anyone write down what happened and what changes because of it?
KSI-INR-AAR.in_place: Every incident above a stated threshold produces a dated report naming what happened, what caused it, what it affected, and the specific changes being made — each with an owner and a date. Blameless, because a report people are punished for produces reports nobody writes.
KSI-INR-AAR.evidence: The reports themselves, with the changes traceable to tickets that were actually closed.
KSI-INR-AAR.check: Query the incident system for incidents closed without a linked report, and for report actions still open past their date. Both are named. What the query cannot assess is whether a report identified the real cause or a convenient one, which is why a person still reads them.

KSI-INR-RPI.question: Do you look back across incidents for patterns, or handle each one and move on?
KSI-INR-RPI.in_place: A periodic review across incidents rather than within one, asking what keeps recurring and which causes were never addressed. The value is in the repeats, which are invisible when each incident is closed in isolation.
KSI-INR-RPI.evidence: A dated review naming what recurred and what was done about the pattern rather than the instance.
KSI-INR-RPI.check: The input is queryable — cluster incidents by cause and count repeats. The review itself is human, and is recorded as a dated artifact.

KSI-MLA-RVL.question: Is anyone actually looking at the logs, or are they only being kept?
KSI-MLA-RVL.in_place: A stated review cadence with a named reviewer, alerting on defined conditions so the routine case does not depend on somebody reading, and a record that the review happened. Retention without review satisfies a storage requirement and no security one.
KSI-MLA-RVL.evidence: Review records with dates and reviewer. The alert rules in force. Response times on what the alerts raised.
KSI-MLA-RVL.check: Query the log platform for review and alert activity. Two failures matter: the newest review older than the cadence, and a log source that silently stopped reporting. The second is more dangerous, because an absence of alerts looks identical to an absence of problems.

KSI-PER-SCR.question: Are people screened before they get access, and does their access actually end when they leave?
KSI-PER-SCR.in_place: Screening completed before access is granted, not after. Separation triggers revocation across every system inside a stated window, driven from the HR record rather than from somebody remembering to file a ticket.
KSI-PER-SCR.evidence: Screening records for people with access. Per departure, the time between separation and revocation in each system.
KSI-PER-SCR.check: Join HR separations to live identity records. Anyone separated who still has an account is named. This is the single most common real path into these environments and it is one query. The screening half is human: a record that a check was completed is an artifact somebody files, not a state a machine can read.

KSI-PIY-RES.question: Does leadership actually look at this, or was it delegated once and forgotten?
KSI-PIY-RES.in_place: A named executive reviews security posture on a stated cadence, and the decisions taken are recorded — including decisions to accept a risk, which is a legitimate outcome that needs a name attached to it.
KSI-PIY-RES.evidence: A dated record naming who attended, what was reviewed, and what was decided.
KSI-PIY-RES.check: Not automatable, and pretending otherwise would be the original mistake in miniature. Record it as a dated artifact with names.

KSI-PIY-RIS.question: Is anyone checking that what you spend on security matches the risks you say you have?
KSI-PIY-RIS.in_place: A periodic review comparing where money and effort actually went against the risk register. The useful finding is usually a well-funded control for a risk nobody rates, sitting next to an unfunded one that everybody does.
KSI-PIY-RIS.evidence: The dated review and what was reprioritised because of it.
KSI-PIY-RIS.check: Not automatable. The inputs — the risk register and the spend — can both be exported, but the comparison is judgment.

KSI-PIY-RSD.question: Does security show up while software is being built, or only after it ships?
KSI-PIY-RSD.in_place: Security requirements enter at design rather than review. Gates in the pipeline enforce the parts that can be enforced. Somebody checks periodically that the gates actually fire rather than having been disabled during a bad week.
KSI-PIY-RSD.evidence: The gate configuration. A sample of features with their security review trail. Evidence that gates fired, including something they blocked.
KSI-PIY-RSD.check: Query the build system for required checks across repositories. Repositories without them are named. The mechanical part stops there. Whether security genuinely entered at design, rather than being bolted on before release, is answered by reading a sample of feature review trails — a human task the gate configuration cannot stand in for.

KSI-PIY-RVD.question: If somebody outside your company finds a hole in your systems, is there a way for them to tell you, and does anyone answer?
KSI-PIY-RVD.in_place: A published intake — an address or form somebody can actually find — with a stated commitment on how fast you will respond, and submissions tracked to closure. Researchers who cannot reach you disclose somewhere else.
KSI-PIY-RVD.evidence: The published policy. The submission log with time to first response and time to fix.
KSI-PIY-RVD.check: Query the intake for submissions past the stated response commitment. Open submissions past the window are named. The human part is quality of response: an intake with zero submissions in a year is worth investigating rather than celebrating, because it usually means nobody can find it.

KSI-SCB-ACT.question: Do you know which machines and services touch controlled information, and is that list current rather than something assembled for the last audit?
KSI-SCB-ACT.in_place: Every asset carries a category — handles controlled information, provides security for those that do, out of scope — maintained from a live inventory rather than a spreadsheet. Categories change when the environment does.
KSI-SCB-ACT.evidence: The categorised inventory with a date, and the source it was reconciled against.
KSI-SCB-ACT.check: Query the inventory and reconcile against what the identity and endpoint platforms actually see. Assets present in the estate but absent from the inventory are named. This measurement is upstream of most others, because a wrong inventory quietly makes every coverage number wrong.

KSI-SCB-DFD.question: Can you show where controlled information actually flows — and was that picture generated from the environment, or drawn by hand and never revisited?
KSI-SCB-DFD.in_place: The diagram is produced from the asset and flow inventory and regenerated on a cadence, so it changes when the environment does. A hand-drawn diagram is accurate on the day it is drawn and decorative afterwards.
KSI-SCB-DFD.evidence: The diagram, the timestamp it was generated, and the source data it came from.
KSI-SCB-DFD.check: Regenerate and diff against the previous version. Flows appearing in network telemetry but not in the diagram are undeclared, and those are the interesting ones — they are how controlled information leaves a boundary nobody realised was open.
